title: What makes a violin sound like a violin?

elements.text: What makes a violin sound like a violin?

commands.speak: Same note, violin or flute, and nobody confuses them — so the thing we call an instrument's voice is not the pitch at all.
The four strings do just one job: they set the pitch.
Open G, D, A and E — and a string on its own is nearly silent, too thin to push much air.
The bow never glides: the rosin grips the string, drags it sideways, and lets it snap back, hundreds of times a second.
That grab-and-release makes a jagged sawtooth wriggle, crowded with overtones, and it runs straight into the bridge.
The bridge rocks on its feet and hands the whole crowd of overtones to the wooden box.
The f-holes let the air inside breathe in and out — a resonance tuned near the open D string.
And the box is no neutral amplifier: wood and air lift some overtones and swallow others, which is the whole trick.
A bare fundamental, no overtones: thin, and like nothing in particular.
Weight the overtones the way a violin body does, and an instrument appears — identical pitch, different voice.
Violins swell a broad band near three thousand hertz, exactly where our ears are sharpest — one violin can ride over sixty players.

Measure the old Cremona instruments and their f-holes are longer and narrower than the round holes that came before — a slow drift toward more sound per hole, over generations of makers copying whatever worked.
So the string chooses the note, and the body chooses the sound — which is why a great violin is a great box, not a great string.
